subject: Chemistry
title: The Chemistry of Fire
description: A quick win: understand The Chemistry of Fire.

hook.text: Fire isn't a thing—it's a process. It's the visible result of a rapid chemical reaction called combustion.

buildup.text: Combustion needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and heat. Remove any one and the fire dies.

discovery.text: When fuel burns, it reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water, heat, and light.

twist.text: Humans controlled fire over a million years ago. But we didn't understand the chemistry until the 1770s.

climax.text: Lavoisier proved combustion was a reaction with oxygen, killing the old 'phlogiston' theory.

punchline.text: Fire isn't magic. It's oxygen grabbing electrons from fuel.

quiz.question: What three things does combustion require?

details.summary: Fire is a rapid exothermic oxidation reaction that requires fuel, oxygen, and heat, known as the fire triangle. The visible flame is incandescent gas, and the color depends on the temperature and the chemical species being oxidized during combustion.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding fire chemistry enables safer building design, better firefighting strategies, and cleaner combustion engines that reduce pollution.
takeaways: Fire requires fuel, oxygen, and heat to sustain itself
Flame color indicates temperature and chemical composition
Removing any side of the fire triangle extinguishes the flame

faq.question: Why do different materials produce different colored flames?
faq.answer: Each element emits photons at characteristic wavelengths when its electrons are excited by heat. Copper produces green flames, sodium produces yellow, and potassium produces violet. This principle underlies both fireworks design and analytical flame tests.

faq.question: Can fire exist without visible flames?
faq.answer: Yes. Hydrogen and methanol burn with nearly invisible flames because their combustion products do not emit strongly in the visible spectrum. This makes certain chemical fires particularly dangerous in laboratory and industrial settings.
